findings.text: Timer creation entries accept a clock selector, an optional user notification description, and an output identifier pointer. When a description pointer is present they copy or convert it from user space and then delegate to a shared creator; otherwise they delegate with no description. Copy failure reports a user memory fault.

Timer query, arm, disarm, overrun and delete entries resolve a timer identifier through a scoped lookup that fails when absent. Get paths zero a kernel setting, fill it via the owning clock operations, then copy to native or 32-bit user form. Set paths fetch a new specification, optionally return an old one, and delegate validation and arming. Delete invalidates then releases the identifier.

Clock set, get, resolution and adjust entries first map the clock identifier to a clock operations table. Missing tables or missing per-operation handlers fail with invalid or unsupported operation. Otherwise they move a timespec or timex structure between user and kernel and invoke the clock specific handler, propagating copy faults.

Nanosleep entries in native and 32-bit forms validate clock support, fetch and validate a requested duration, suppress any remainder pointer for absolute waits, install a non-restarting restart block describing remainder flavour and pointer, then dispatch to the clock sleep handler.

Shared timer helpers implement remaining-time query, forward-by-interval, arm, cancel attempt, wait-for-handler, set, delete and exit cleanup. They operate on an already looked-up timer object and its owning clock operations, updating interval, expiry state and overrun accounting.

Time conversion helpers move interval timer specifications and frequency control structures between kernel 64-bit form and native or legacy 32-bit user forms. Interval helpers transfer interval then value; frequency helpers transfer a fixed field set including modes, offsets, error estimates, status and counters.

Only identifiers within the positive signed integer range can resolve; larger values fail lookup without further action. A successful lookup additionally requires that the timer still belongs to the caller signal context, checked both without locks and again while holding the timer lock.

Query reports interval when periodic. One-shot disarmed timers with real delivery return an empty value without consulting the clock. Periodic timers that are not marked armed, or that request no notification, first advance expiry and accumulate overruns so the next expiry lies after the sampled now; remaining time is then derived from that same now sample.

Query of an expired one-shot distinguishes delivery mode: no-notification timers report zero remaining, while timers with real delivery still report a minimal positive remaining because delivery has not happened. Consequently periodic timers never report expired remaining after forwarding.

Arming snapshots old state when requested, attempts cancellation, marks disarmed, installs the new interval and value, and leaves disarmed when the new value is zero. Non-zero values are converted to kernel time, translated for absolute waits in namespaces, then armed; immediate expiry queues delivery instead of arming.

Relative realtime timers are run on the monotonic base so later wall clock changes do not shift them, while the stored clock selector is left unchanged so a later absolute arm can switch back. Absolute selection chooses the realtime base; relative selection chooses monotonic for realtime clocks.

Set validates both interval and value as normalized timespecs and rejects invalid ones. Absolute sleeps and absolute timer values use absolute expiry mode and namespace translation where applicable; relative waits use relative mode. Absolute sleep never returns a remainder.

No-notification timers are treated as logically queued without starting the underlying high resolution timer. Their status is left disarmed on arm, yet query and forward logic still advances them and handles expiry specially.

Lookup holds a read-side critical section across hash lookup so the object cannot be freed, then acquires the per-timer interrupt-saving spinlock and revalidates ownership before returning with that lock held. Failure drops the lock and returns absent.

Deletion fences delivery by bumping a sequence count, then under the signal handler lock marks the owner pointer invalid, removes the timer from the signal list with ordered removal, and drops any ignored-list link. Cancellation retries until it no longer reports busy, releasing and reacquiring the timer lock around a wait for a running handler.

Set protects against concurrent delivery and rearming by bumping a sequence count while holding the timer lock. When the clock reports busy it retains a read-side hold, drops the scoped lookup, waits for any running handler without touching the timer afterwards, then retries without returning a stale old value.

Task exit detaches the whole signal timer list under the signal handler lock with interrupts saved, so concurrent readers observe an empty list. Each detached timer is then deleted under its own timer lock and its identifier released, yielding the processor between timers. Leftover ignored links are drained separately and their absence is asserted.

Timers move between disarmed and armed. Cancel and new-setting install force disarmed; successful arm of a notifying timer marks armed; immediate expiry queues a signal instead; delete forces disarmed. Overrun counts missed periodic expiries discovered during forward and are exposed through a bounded integer conversion.

Object lifetime proceeds from hash insertion in an invalid owner state, to valid after initialization, to invalidated under locks during delete, to hash removal and reference release, to deferred reclamation after a grace period. Queued delivery can extend the reference beyond hash removal; final release happens on delivery or flush.

The kernel timer object carries an identifier, a clock selector, a pointer to the active clock operations, a per-timer lock, an owner signal pointer, a sequence fence, notification mode, interval and status, overrun count, signal queue state, list links for signal and ignored lists, and an embedded high resolution timer.

The clock operations table provides wall and monotonic accessors, remaining and forward helpers, get, set, delete, arm, cancel and wait callbacks for timers, plus set, get, resolution, adjust and sleep handlers for clocks. Timer code dispatches remaining, forward, arm, cancel, wait, get and set through it; syscall entries dispatch clock operations through it.

Interval settings consist of an interval plus a value, each a seconds plus nanoseconds pair, in both 64-bit kernel form and native or legacy 32-bit user forms. Frequency control carries scalar tuning fields plus a second plus microsecond time pair and counter fields, again with kernel and legacy user layouts.

User memory failures during fetch or store of event descriptions, timer settings, timespecs and frequency structures fail the call with a fault status and without changing timer or clock state. Missing user pointers for new settings, unknown clocks, missing handlers and malformed durations fail with invalid or unsupported operation as appropriate.

Expiry handlers may spin on the timer lock on multiprocessors, so set, delete and exit paths must tolerate busy cancellation and never touch the object after waiting for a running handler. Sequence fencing plus owner invalidation prevents use after free, duplicate delivery, rearming after delete, and premature identifier reuse while a lookup still observes the old object.

Behaviour is keyed by absolute-time selection, no-notification delivery, realtime clock identity, absolute versus relative high resolution modes, armed versus disarmed status, a busy-retry status, and native versus compat versus no-remainder sleep types. Identifiers are bounded by the maximum positive signed integer.

User-visible failures use fault for bad user addresses, invalid argument for unknown clocks, missing pointers and malformed times, and not-supported for clocks lacking adjust or sleep. Resolution queries tolerate a null output pointer and succeed after computing the value.
